newsitem.title: INDIA: India to offer reward for news of Western hostages.
newsitem.headline: India to offer reward for news of Western hostages.

text.p: India will offer a one million rupee ($28,000) reward for news of four Western hostages taken captive 17 months ago, a senior police official in northern Jammu and Kashmir state said on Thursday.

"We will distribute posters with the black-and-white pictures of the hostages, asking people for authentic information about the location of the hostages in return for a one-million-rupee reward," the official told Reuters.

Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Farooq Abdullah said in November that his state government planned to offer a reward for the information, shortly after New Delhi turned down a proposal by the United States to make such a move.
Americans Donald Hutchings and John Childs and Britons Keith Mangan and Paul Wells were kidnapped by Al-Faran militants while hiking in the Kashmiri mountains on July 4, 1995.
Childs escaped four days later and Al-Faran captured Norwegian Hans-Christian Ostroe and German Dirk Hasert. A month later, Ostroe was found beheaded in a remote Kashmiri forest.
Negotiations between Indian officials and Al-Faran broke down in November 1995.
Since then, local Kashmiris have periodically reported sighting the four remaining hostages, but authorities have not been able to determine with certainty whether the captives are dead or alive.

U.S. diplomats said in October they hoped to tap a government programme that offers up to $2 million for information that can be used to combat acts of "terrorism" aimed at citizens abroad for a reward for news of the hostages.
But Indian authorities opposed the move. Soon after, Abdullah declared his government's intention to offer a reward.
The police official, who declined to be identified, said the posters would be put up in the south Kashmir area where the hostages were kidnapped.
"We will distribute the posters, particularly in south Kashmir, in Pahalgam and Doda," the official said.
"They will give the numbers of two telephones in Sringar, two in Jammu and one in New Delhi, so that people can call with information," he said. "Their identities will be protected."
Authorities used sniffer dogs in June to search a forest where a captured militant said he believed the hostages had been buried after being killed last year. But they found no clues.
Al-Faran had not been heard of before the kidnappings. Dozens of guerrilla groups are fighting Indian rule in Jammu and Kashmir, the predominantly Hindu nation's only Moslem majority state.
Police and hospital say more than 20,000 people have died in the six-year-old revolt. Abdullah puts the figure closer to 50,000.
